title: Paspalum scrobiculatum: How to Spot and Control This Rice Field Grass
metaTitle: Paspalum scrobiculatum in Rice: ID and Control Guide
metaDescription: Paspalum scrobiculatum, or kodo millet, invades rainfed palay. Learn its local names, how to spot it early and how to keep it out of your rice field.
excerpt: Paspalum scrobiculatum is an annual grass weed of rainfed lowland rice fields in the Philippines. Its English name is kodo millet. It grows from seed and fights your palay for light, water and fertilizer. This page shows how to spot it in the field and how to control it before it drops seed.

heroImage.alt: Kodo millet (Paspalum scrobiculatum), a grass weed of Philippine rice fields
heroImage.credit: David Eickhoff from Pearl City, Hawaii, USA, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
This damo is a grass from the Poaceae family, the same family as palay. Farmers know it as bias biasin, angangsug or sabung sabungan. In India, farmers grow the same species as a grain called kodo millet. Here at home, Paspalum scrobiculatum turns up as a weed in rainfed lowland rice fields, where the water comes from rain alone.

It is an annual, so each plant lives for only one season. It spreads by seed, and its stems do not creep along the ground to root at the joints. Every plant that flowers drops fresh seeds into the soil. Those seeds then wait for the next planting. So the best time to stop it is before its seed heads turn reddish brown.

Like all grasses, this weed has a round, hollow stem with nodes, or joints, along its length. The stems are smooth and slender, with a purplish color near the base. They stand up instead of creeping. Leaf blades are flat and narrow, and their edges feel rough between your fingers. The leaf sheath is dark green and hairy close to the blade. Where the blade meets the sheath, look for a long, brown, papery ligule.

items: Stem bases turn purplish, while the rest of the slender stem stays smooth.
Run a finger along the leaf edge and you will feel that it is rough.
Seed heads carry three to four spike like branches set one after another along the stalk.
Spikelets sit in two neat rows, round to egg shaped, pale at first and reddish brown later.
Tiny purple stigmas peek out of the spikelets when the plant is in flower.
The plant stands upright and never roots along the ground like a creeping grass.

blocks.text:
Like other grass weeds, Paspalum scrobiculatum competes with palay for sunlight, water and fertilizer. Because it is a grass too, its young plants can look a lot like rice seedlings. As a result, some plants slip past early weeding and keep feeding on nutrients meant for your crop.

Once it flowers, it drops seed that adds to the weed seed bank in your soil. Then the problem grows a little bigger each season. Its seeds can also mix with harvested palay and lower the quality of seed you keep for planting. Thick stands give shelter to rats and insect pests close to the rice hills, too.

items: Keep water standing in the paddy whenever the rains allow, because a flooded soil surface holds back many grass seeds from sprouting.
Pull young plants by hand before seed heads appear. It spreads by seed only, so no flowering plant means no new seed.
Weed the bunds and field edges as well, because plants left there shed seed that washes back into the paddy.
After harvest, cut or pull any plants still standing before they drop seed, so the next crop starts cleaner.

blocks.text: What to Do at Each Age of Your Rice

items: **0 to 5 days:** keep the soil saturated. Use a pre emergence herbicide only if the field had many weeds last season.
**6 to 10 days:** hand weed in transplanted rice. In direct seeded rice, this is the window for an early post emergence spray.
**11 to 20 days:** keep water in the field, weed by hand or with a rotary weeder, and let Azolla and the Altica beetle help. Spray only if those fail.
**21 to 30 days:** top up the water and keep weeding. Spray only if weeding fails.
**31 to 40 days (transplanted rice):** hand weed. A spray this late is only a rescue.
After any post emergence spray, bring the water back within 1 to 3 days at 3 to 5 cm and hold it for 4 to 5 days. Keep young rice above it.

blocks.text: Active Ingredients That Work on Grasses

If water and weeding cannot hold Paspalum scrobiculatum down, choose an active ingredient that works on grasses at the age of your rice. The table follows the PhilRice eDamuhan recommendations. Shop by the ingredient on the label, never by the brand. If your field also has other kinds of weeds, the [weed control helper](/weeds#control) finds the ingredients that cover all of them.

blocks.text: Use only herbicides registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label on the pack: the rate, the timing, the water and the protective clothing. Switch herbicide groups between seasons so the weeds do not learn to survive them. Our [guide to herbicides for rice](/weeds/herbicides-for-rice-weeds) explains the groups.
Keep Paspalum scrobiculatum Out Next Season

items: Plant clean, certified seed. Weed seeds mixed into the punla are the easiest way in.
Keep the seedbed, the canals and the bunds free of weeds, so seed does not wash or blow into the paddy.
Prepare the land well: flood, plow, let the weed seeds sprout, then kill them when you harrow. Level the field so water covers it evenly.
Pull escapes before the seed heads open, and clean the thresher and harvester before they enter the field.
Keep the field clean after harvest and through the fallow, so fewer seeds build up in the soil for next season.

blocks.text: These steps work for every [grass weed](/weeds/types-of-weeds) in the paddy, not only this one. The [weed management guide](/weeds/weed-management-in-rice) puts them in order for a whole season.
Not Sure It Is Paspalum scrobiculatum?

Take a clear photo of the leaf, the stem and the flower or seed head, then ask [Anee, the smart farm technician](/features/ai-agricultural-technician) in anee.io, in Tagalog or English. blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Paspalum scrobiculatum

items.q: What do Filipino farmers call Paspalum scrobiculatum?
items.a: Farmers call it bias biasin, angangsug or sabung sabungan. In English it goes by kodo millet, since the same species grows as a grain crop in India. It belongs to the grass family, Poaceae. When you ask a technician for help, give one of these local names or show a photo of the reddish brown seed heads.

items.q: How do I control this grass in my rice field?
items.a: Start with clean seed and a well leveled field so water covers the soil evenly. Keep the paddy flooded when the rain allows. Next, pull young plants by hand before they flower. If you need a herbicide, choose one made for grass weeds that fits the age of your rice. Always follow the FPA registered label.

items.q: Why does it keep coming back every season?
items.a: It comes back from seed. Each plant that flowers drops seeds into the soil, and some stay there until the next land preparation. So even a few plants left to flower can start a new flush of weeds. Weed before flowering every season, and over time you will have fewer seeds waiting in the soil.
